figures.caption: Internalization and subcellular localization of MtDef4 in Botrytis cinerea. (a) Time‐lapse confocal microscopy images showing internalization of DyLight‐550 labelled MtDef4 in B. cinerea germlings. Images were captured every 3 min for 1 h and those taken at 21, 24, 27, 33 and 39 min were shown. (b) Enlarged 24‐min image in (a) highlighted by the red frame. Entry spots are indicated by white arrows and the assumed nucleus is indicated by red arrows. (c,i) Subcellular localization of MtDef4 in B. cinerea germlings (c) and spores (i). Spores and germlings that emerged from overnight germination of spores were treated with 1.5 μM DyLight550‐MtDef4 for 60 and 30 min, respectively, and incubated with 4′,6‐diamidino‐2‐phenylindole (DAPI) and FM4‐64 for another 15 min. (d,j) Signal intensity taken from ROI.01 from (c) and ROI.02 from (i). Yellow arrows indicate the overlapping signal of DyLight550‐MtDef4 and FM4‐64, and the purple arrows indicate the overlapping signal of DyLight550‐MtDef4 and DAPI. (e–h, k–n) Fluorescence signal of DyLight550‐MtDef4 and FM4‐64 (e,k) and DyLight550‐MtDef4 and DAPI (g,m). The overlapping signal (DyLight550‐MtDef4 and FM4‐64, f and l; DyLight550‐MtDef4 and DAPI, h and n) is shown in the right panel as white pixels and considered as colocalized area. The threshold for each channel is 30% and for the background is 20%. Confocal microscopy SP8 was used to take images and the excitation and emission wavelength of DyLight550 was 555 nm, 580–620 nm, DAPI was 405 nm, 415–460 nm and FM4‐64 was 555 nm, 680–800 nm. LAX software was used to quantify the signal intensity and the graphs were illustrated by GraphPad Prism v. 8.0. Scale bars = 10 μm.

figures.caption: Ultrastructural effects of high‐pressure freezing and freeze–substitution of MtDef4‐treated Botrytis cinerea. (a) Transmission electron microscopy images of germling tips of untreated B. cinerea showed a normal complement of organelles including an accumulation of vesicles at the Spitzenkörper (S), mitochondria (M), actin‐coated filasomes (arrowheads) and a smooth plasma membrane profile. (b) A germling tip after 60 min MtDef4 treatment (1.5 μM) with moderate effects showed numerous electron‐dense plasma membrane anomalies (arrows), nucleus (N) and filasomes (arrowheads). (B1) Some membrane invaginations (arrows) exhibited a ribosome‐free fibrillar zone reminiscent of filasome initials, while others (B2) had complex membrane whorls. Some 60 min‐treated germling tips (c) and distil regions (d) showed severe cellular effects including a highly convoluted plasma membrane (arrows), an irregular outer fibrillar coating on the cell wall (asterisk), dense cytoplasm, swollen and reduced electron density in mitochondria (M), expanded lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear (N) envelope and prominent vacuolization (V). (a, b, c, d, scale bars = 1 μm; B1 & B2, scale bars = 0.25 μm).
figures.label: FIGURE 2

figures.caption: MtDef4‐interacting proteins in Botrytis cinerea enriched in ribosomes and protein translation. (a) SDS‐PAGE and silver staining of the elution fractions from MagStrep type3 XT beads of MtDef4‐StrepII or Strep II tag incubated with total protein extracted from B. cinerea mycelium (left panel). The total protein extracted was run on SDS‐PAGE gel and stained using InstantBlue (right panel). The molecular weight markers are shown on the left. (b) Gene ontology enrichment analysis of the MtDef4‐binding proteins identified by liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). The horizontal axis indicates the number of proteins identified in each category shown on the vertical axis. The categories with more than two proteins are shown. (c) SDS‐PAGE and silver staining of the elution fractions from MagStrep type3 XT beads of MtDef4‐StrepII or Strep II tag treated with crude ribosome extracted from B. cinerea. The molecular weight markers are indicated on the left. (d) Relative translational activity of the in vitro translation system in the presence of 50 μM MtDef4 and MtDef4‐StrepII. The translation products were detected at 0, 10, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min. Sterile water was used as a negative control (the translation activity was set to 1) and cycloheximide was used as a positive control. (e) Relative translation activity of the in vitro translation system in the presence of different antimicrobial peptides is shown as a bar plot (mean ± SD) that is overlaid with individual data points. Each peptide (50 μM) was incubated with the translation system for 1 h. The translation activity without antimicrobial peptides was set to 1.
figures.label: FIGURE 3

figures.caption: Sequences, antifungal activity of MtDef4, variants and truncated peptides, and the translation imbibition activity. (a) Amino acid sequences of MtDef4, its Ala substitution variants and truncated peptides. The secondary structure is shown on top. The green wavy line, blue arrow and straight line indicate α‐helix, β‐sheet and random coil, respectively. The γ‐core motifs are highlighted by a red frame. The amino acid substitutions are shown in red. The fold reduction of antifungal activity against Botrytis cinerea (B.c) and Fusarium graminearum (F.g) is shown on the right as a heat map. Darker blue indicates more loss of antifungal activity compared with that of MtDef4 and white indicates no change. (b) Translation activity of the in vitro translation system in the presence of MtDef4, MtDef4 variants and truncated peptides at different concentrations. The translation products were quantitatively determined after 1 h translation. Data are shown as mean ± SD. (c) Binding assay of ribosomes with MtDef4 and MtDef4_V4. Ribosomes (5 μg) from B. cinerea were incubated with 2 μg MtDef4 or MtDef4_V4 for 30 min, followed by centrifugation at 200,000 g for 2 h. After extensive washings, MtDef4 and MtDef4_V4 were immunodetected using the anti‐MtDef4 antibody. Anti‐RPL12 was used to determine the presence of ribosomes in each component. S: supernatant, P: pellet. (d) The relative signal intensity of the protein co‐precipitated with ribosomes (labelled as * in c) was determined by western blot analysis. The signal from 100 ng of each pure protein was used as the reference. Data are shown as mean ± SD. Significant analysis was performed by unpaired two‐tailed t test (n = 3). p < 0.05 indicates a significant difference.
figures.label: FIGURE 4

figures.caption: The semi‐in planta antifungal activity of MtDef4, its variants and truncated peptides against Botrytis cinerea on detached Nicotiana benthamiana leaves and rose petals. (a,c) Different concentrations of peptides were applied onto the surface of leaves or petals and an equal volume of the B. cinerea conidia was applied to the same spot immediately at the final concentration of 105 spores/mL. The inoculated tissues were kept in the Ziploc boxes to maintain high humidity. Plant tissues treated with water instead of peptides and spores were set as controls. Images were taken at 48 h post‐inoculation. (b,d) Quantification of the lesion sizes shown in a and c, respectively. Lesion sizes were measured using ImageJ and the relative lesion sizes are shown as mean ± SD. The data were compared with the control to determine if the difference was significant using the unpaired two‐tailed t test (ns, p > 0.05, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001) by Prism GraphPad.

figures.caption: Sequences, solvent accessible surface and antifungal activity of MtDef4, MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6. (a) Amino acids sequences of MtDef4, MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6. The substituted amino acids are shown in red. The predicted amino acids participating in forming the positively charged pocket are highlighted in bold font. (b) Three‐dimensional structure of MtDef4, and predicted structures of MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6. 3D structures of MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6 were predicted using AlphaFold2 Colab (AlphaFold2.ipynb). The NMR structure of MtDef4 (PDB: 2LR3) was used as a template. Structures and their solvent‐accessible surface with potential charge were visualized by PyMOL (v. 2.0 Schrödinger, LLC). The white surface regions represent zero net charge and the blue colour indicates the positively charged regions. The predicted cationic pockets are highlighted using a red circle. The semitransparent molecular surface in the right panel shows the amino acids potentially participating in forming this pocket, which is highlighted as red sticks. In MtDef4, Ser16 and Asp17 are shown as black sticks. (c) Antifungal activity of peptides in the presence of 100 mM KCl or 2 mM CaCl2 was determined using resazurin cell viability assay. Different concentrations (0.75–6 μM) of peptides were incubated with Botrytis cinerea spores for 48 h. Images were taken after adding resazurin at 0.01% (wt/vol) for overnight incubation. The metabolically active cells can degrade resazurin and the colour changes to pink or colourless. (d) Representative microscopy images of B. cinerea treated with 1.5 μM MtDef4, MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6 in the presence of 100 mM KCl or 2 mM CaCl2. Images were taken 48 h after incubation with peptides. The images showing the effects of peptides on fungal growth at other concentrations are shown in Figure S10. Scale bar = 100 μm.

figures.caption: The interaction of MtDef4 and MtDef4_V6 with chitin and β‐glucan. (a) Confocal microscopy images of Botrytis cinerea germlings and conidia treated with DyLight550‐MtDef4 and DyLight550‐MtDef4_V6 for 30 min, respectively. FM4‐64 was added 15 min in advance of taking images to stain membranes. Arrowheads point out the cell surface region. Scale bars = 10 μm. (b) DyLight550‐MtDef4 (red line) and FM4‐64 (green line) signal intensity of ROI.01 to ROI.04 in (a). (c,d) SDS‐PAGE and InstantBlue‐stained gel showing the interaction of MtDef4 or MtDef4_V6 with chitin (c) and β‐glucan (d). Different concentrations of insoluble carbohydrates of cell wall components, chitin and β‐glucan, were incubated with 6 μM MtDef4 or MtDef4_V6 for 1 h at 4°C. After centrifugation, peptides left in the supernatant were loaded onto the gel. (e,f) The dissociation constants of chitin and β‐glucan binding based on the gel from three independent replications were calculated using non‐linear regression with a one‐site binding model. Data are shown as mean ± SD. (g) Summary of the binding affinity of MtDef4 or MtDef4_V6 to chitin and β‐glucan, respectively.
figures.label: FIGURE 7

figures.caption: MtDef4_V6 confers greater protection against the grey mould disease in planta. (a–c) The semi‐in planta antifungal activity of MtDef4, MtDef4_V5 and MtDef4_V6 on Nicotiana benthamiana leaves, rose petals and tomato fruits. The concentration of each peptide is 3 μM on N. benthamiana leaves, 0.75 μM on rose petals and 12 μM on tomato fruits. Each peptide was applied on the surface of plant tissue and fresh conidia of Botrytis cinerea at 5 × 104/mL were applied immediately at the same spot. Images of N. benthamiana leaves and rose petals were taken 48 h post‐inoculation (hpi) and those of tomato fruits 60 hpi. (d) Quantitative analysis of the relative lesion sizes shown in a–c. The lesion size formed without peptide treatment was set as 1. One‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to perform statistical analysis, (**p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ns, p > 0.05, n = 3). Bars = mean ± SD. (e) N. benthamiana plants sprayed with peptides and inoculated with B. cinerea spores. Two‐week‐old N. benthamiana plants were sprayed with 12 μM MtDef4 or MtDef4_V6 and B. cinerea spores at 8 × 104/mL by spraying on the plant's surface. Plants challenged with fungal spores alone and those sprayed with water alone were set as controls. The peptide solution or water was allowed to dry out on the surface of leaves (approx. 2 h) before sprayed by B. cinerea spores. Images were captured at about 72 hpi. (f) The enlarged view of leaves in (e) shows lesions. (g) Quantitative analysis of the calculated photosynthetic quantum yield (Fv/Fm) for individual N. benthamiana plants shown as a box plot. One‐way analysis of variance was used to determine the statistical difference among treatments (*p < 0.05, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001, ns, p > 0.05, n = 4).
figures.label: FIGURE 8

figures.caption: A proposed model for the antifungal action of MtDef4 in killing Botrytis cinerea. MtDef4 binds β‐glucan and chitin in the cell wall and phospholipids of the cell membrane. Subsequently, peptides are able to penetrate the plasma membrane and internalize into the cytoplasm and nucleus. MtDef4 specifically binds to ribosomes and inhibits translation causing cell death. Membrane disruption and interaction with other intracellular targets are hypothesized to contribute to fungal cell killing as well.
